title: The third step
hookLine: the small boy grows past the clouds, and a king offers his own head
carry: atma-nivedana: offering yourself, not just your things
tomorrow: a sage's son with a warrior's axe. how did that happen?
last: THE EARTH CAN'T CARRY A LIAR.

cards: A time-lapse video squeezes a whole season of a seed becoming a tree into a few seconds. This is faster. The water touches the ground, and the boy begins to grow.
Past the sacrifice ground, past the clouds, until in the telling the sun and stars are no higher than his waist. One stride covers the earth. A second covers the heavens.
Then he turns to the king and asks: where do I put the third?

teach.b: In the Bhagavata, this giant form is called Trivikrama, the one of the three strides. It's an old picture: a hymn in the Rig Veda already praises Vishnu for measuring out the worlds in three steps.
The Purana turns that hymn into a story with a person at the end of it. Two strides have taken everything Bali owns. And Vishnu presses him: you promised three.
Bali doesn't argue and doesn't beg.
He bows and says: put your third step on my head. Then Prahlada arrives, the boy from the man-lion's story, now Bali's grandfather, and he doesn't grieve.
He calls it grace: the riches are gone, and the pride that came with them. Vishnu agrees.
He sends Bali to rule Sutala, a world below, and makes a promise that turns the whole story over: he will stand guard at Bali's own door. So the story doesn't end with a king crushed.
It ends with a king who ran out of things to give, and gave himself.

In this same Purana, Prahlada names nine ways of bhakti, devotion: hearing about God, singing, remembering, serving, worship, bowing, being God's servant, being God's friend, and the last, atma-nivedana, offering your very self.
Later teachers point to Bali as the model of that last one. Bhakti can start with a flower. Its far end is a bowed head saying: not just what I have.

how: Images of Trivikrama, one foot raised high mid-stride, are carved on temple walls, and in Kerala the festival of Onam welcomes Mahabali back to visit his people.

o: Vishnu's small form who grew and took three strides
the king who gave away three steps of ground
a world below where a king is sent to rule

games.q: the three strides — tap the pairs.
p: the world Bali is sent to rule

s: Vamana's story ends with Bali crushed and punished
Vishnu sends him to rule Sutala and promises to guard his door.
a Rig Veda hymn already praises Vishnu's three strides
the Purana turns that old picture into a story.
the last of the nine ways of bhakti Prahlada names is offering yourself
atma-nivedana. later teachers point to Bali, head bowed, as its model.

games.q: at the temple, an auntie smiles at your offering: just one flower. by Bali's story, what counts most in bhakti?
o: what you give of yourself; Bali's last gift was his own head.
the size of the gift; Bali was loved for giving away the worlds.
getting the ritual exactly right; that's what his guru cared about.
games.why: two strides took the worlds; what Vishnu answered was the third, Bali bowing. in the Gita, Krishna says it too: a leaf, a flower, offered with love, he accepts.

practice: If you pray, bow your head the way many Hindus do at the end of puja, and offer not a thing but yourself: here I am. If you don't pray, simply bow a little and let the back of your neck soften.
Rest there for the sit, the weight of your head held, nothing to defend. If your neck tires, lift it slowly and let your shoulders do the bowing.

wordCard.voice: Vamana: Vishnu's small form, who grew to stride across the worlds and took his third step on Bali's bowed head.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the one of the three strides, Vishnu's giant form in the Vamana story.

carryVoice: Keep this one: atma-nivedana, offering yourself, not just your things. Bali's bowed head took the third step. A new week, begun.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 8.20–8.23 (Trivikrama's strides; Bali offers his head; Prahlada; Sutala; Vishnu at Bali's door)
Bhagavata Purana 7.5.23–24 (Prahlada names nine ways of bhakti, ending with atma-nivedana, offering oneself)
